positioning.caseStudyRationale: This is reproducible experimental systems research on a live Kubernetes control-plane path, not a report about an organization's production deployment.
positioning.decisionRationale: The primary track explicitly welcomes cloud native research, academic papers, proof-of-concept projects, and advanced niche topics. A 30-minute session can connect the initial validation failure, an equal-budget mitigation experiment, and practical live-system tuning guidance; the poster remains a suitable fallback for the research artifact.

proposal.title: Searching the Kubernetes Scheduler Policy Space: Lessons From Noisy Live Optimization
proposal.sessionDescription:
When a live optimizer reports a better Kubernetes policy, did it improve the system or learn the benchmark noise? This session follows that question through a custom four-weight scheduler, an NSGA-II-style optimizer, and real Pod bindings on a four-worker kind cluster. Each policy sample patches and rolls out the scheduler, replays three 24-Pod resource-pressure workloads, and records scheduler-side decision latency plus workload-occupied workers.

The first search appeared to beat the hand-designed policies across three seeds, but none of its five finalists remained nondominated after ten repetitions on each training workload. The follow-up experiment tests a practical mitigation: spend the same 72 live samples per seed either on one-shot exploration or on a deterministic two-stage strategy that re-evaluates promising policies. Across three seeds, shared validation removes two of three one-shot finalists and one of three two-stage finalists. Holdout testing is stricter: only one of the three survivors remains nondominated, and its apparent latency advantage over the consolidation policy at the same worker count is a 43-microsecond near-tie with overlapping intervals.

The session turns this reversal into an engineering playbook. Attendees will see how policy-space redundancy, timestamp provenance, exact evaluation budgets, immutable artifacts, repeated promotion, and held-out validation affect automated tuning of a live Kubernetes control loop. The conclusion is not a universally better scheduler; it is a reproducible account of how to detect and reduce false optimization discoveries before deploying them.
proposal.benefitsToEcosystem: Platform teams increasingly use search and automated tuning around scheduling, autoscaling, databases, runtimes, and other live control loops. Those optimizers can exploit timing jitter, equivalent parameters, or incomplete runs as efficiently as they exploit useful system behavior. This session contributes both a failure analysis and a budget-matched mitigation experiment: reserve part of the search budget for re-evaluating promising candidates, then validate all arms under the same repeated protocol. The open experiment also shows how to separate scheduler feasibility from tunable scoring, measure the decision rather than the observer, preserve sample-level provenance, and avoid turning exact Pareto arithmetic into an unsupported superiority claim.
proposal.targetAudience: Kubernetes platform engineers, SREs, scheduler and controller developers, performance engineers, and researchers who evaluate or tune policies against live clusters.
proposal.prerequisites: Attendees should understand basic Kubernetes Pod scheduling and be comfortable reading latency and resource-usage metrics. No prior evolutionary-computation knowledge is required.
takeaways: How to expose a Kubernetes scheduler scoring policy to search without retaining scale-equivalent or linearly redundant weight dimensions.
How to distinguish scheduler decision latency, Kubernetes timestamp resolution, and evaluator observation lag in a live experiment.
Why one evaluation per candidate can create convincing but non-reproducible Pareto improvements, and how to compare exploration with resampling under an equal live-evaluation budget.
How repeated promotion, shared validation, and holdout testing expose false Pareto discoveries without overstating near-ties as scheduler superiority.

outline.topic: The real question: policy improvement or measurement-noise optimization?
A live custom scheduler, evaluator, and real Pod-binding loop
Policy-space failure: scale equivalence, redundant packing, and the V2 repair
Measurement repair: decision annotations, observation lag, hard validity gates, and provenance
The apparent win: three seeds, five finalists, zero repeated survivors
The equal-budget mitigation: one-shot exploration versus two-stage resampling
Shared validation, holdout near-tie, and the limits of exact Pareto claims

supportedClaims: The V2 one-shot search evaluated 216 optimizer candidates; none of its five finalists remained nondominated after ten repetitions per policy-workload pair.

The official V3 experiment gave each arm exactly 216 fresh optimizer samples across seeds 42, 123, and 999; together the arms completed 1,350 workload replays and 32,400 Pods without unschedulable results.
Shared ten-repeat validation classified two of three one-shot finalists and one of three two-stage finalists as false Pareto discoveries under the repeated-mean point-estimate rule.
Only one of three shared-validation survivors remained nondominated on the fixed holdout workload.
The holdout survivor and consolidation baseline used the same mean 2.1 workers; their mean p95 difference was about 43 microseconds and their confidence intervals overlapped.
excludedClaims: Evolutionary search found a scheduler that is superior to Kubernetes defaults.
Two-stage resampling is statistically or generally superior to one-shot search.
The surviving optimizer policy is practically superior to the consolidation baseline.
The optimizer finalists generalize beyond the fixed holdout workload.
The kind results establish production-cluster performance.
Maximum workload-occupied workers is equivalent to powered-node cost.
The observed holdout latency means are statistically distinct.

speaker.name: Ismail Tarim
speaker.bio: Ismail Tarim is a student at Izmir Katip Celebi University working at the intersection of Kubernetes systems and evolutionary computation. He built evo-sched as an end-to-end research system that connects a real custom scheduler, reproducible workload replay, experiment provenance, and multi-objective policy search.
